beats.say: Open like a teacher: adding is one of the things we do most, so let's be quick and clever. Say we will learn to spot friendly pairs and to break numbers up. No questions.

lines.say: Look at this: eight plus seven plus two plus three. You could add left to right, but there's a cleverer way, and once you see it, you can't unsee it.

beats.say: Number bonds to 10: 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6, 5+5. Look for pairs that make ten. Then do 8+7+2+3. No questions.

lines.say: First, our friendly pairs that make ten. One and nine, two and eight, three and seven, four and six, five and five. Learn these and sums get easy.
Back to our sum. Do you see any pairs?
Eight and two make ten. Seven and three make ten.
So that's ten plus ten, which is twenty. Much easier than adding one by one.

beats.say: Order and grouping do not change a total: 6+8+4+2. Add in any order. Name it: you can swap or regroup. No questions.

lines.say: Here's another. Six plus eight plus four plus two.
Adding can be done in any order, so I'll pick my pairs: six and four make ten, and eight and two make ten.
Ten and ten make twenty.

lines.text: Adding in any order, or in any groups, gives the same total
lines.say: So adding in any order, or grouping the numbers any way you like, gives the same total. Mathematicians say addition can be swapped and regrouped.

beats.say: Counting on in ones is slow and slips. Compare 27 + 5 counted in ones with bridging to the next ten: 27 + 3 + 2. No questions.

lines.say: Let's add five to twenty-seven. One way: count on in ones. Twenty-eight, twenty-nine, thirty, thirty-one, thirty-two. It works, but it's slow, and it's easy to lose your place.
Here's a smarter way, called bridging. Twenty-seven needs three to reach thirty, so we split the five into three and two. Twenty-seven plus three is thirty.
And thirty plus the two left over is thirty-two.

lines.text: Bridge to the next ten, then add what is left
lines.say: Bridging to the next ten is quick, because adding onto a ten is easy.

beats.say: Written method by partitioning: 46 + 37. Add tens, add ones, then add the two. Mention that column addition is the same idea. No questions.

lines.say: For bigger numbers, we can partition. Forty-six plus thirty-seven.
Split forty-six into forty and six.
And thirty-seven into thirty and seven.
Add the pink tens together: seventy. Add the yellow ones together: thirteen.
And finally join them: seventy plus thirteen is eighty-three. Column addition is exactly this, just written neatly in columns.

beats.say: Do one TOGETHER: 7+3+9+1 by pairs to ten. Questions written on the board first.

lines.say: Now you help me. Seven plus three plus nine plus one. Look for pairs that make ten.
Seven and three.

ask.prompt: Which two numbers here make ten?
ask.onMiss: Ask: what do we add to 7 to get to 10?

lines.say: And nine and one.

ask.onMiss: Ask: what is left after we use 7 and 3?

lines.say: So ten plus ten.

ask.onMiss: Ask: you found two tens. What is ten plus ten?

beats.say: The child works alone: 58 + 25 by partitioning; 4 + 9 + 6 + 1 + 5 by pairs. Hints only if stuck.

lines.say: Your turn to lead. Fifty-eight plus twenty-five. Partition both numbers.

ask.prompt: Work out 58 + 25 by partitioning. Tell me your steps.
ask.onMiss: Ask: what are the tens parts? Then the ones parts?

lines.say: Now a string of numbers: four plus nine plus six plus one plus five.

ask.prompt: Use pairs to ten. What is the total?
ask.onMiss: Ask: which pairs make ten? What is left over?
